learningObjective: Explain the pipeline-parallel bubble and how microbatching reduces it.
stem: A model is split across P=8 pipeline stages, one per GPU. A training step consists of M microbatches processed in a GPipe-style schedule. Which statement about the pipeline bubble is correct?

options.text: The bubble is exactly 1/P of total time regardless of M; it can only be removed by reducing P, which defeats the purpose of pipeline parallelism.
The bubble fraction is approximately (P-1)/(P + M - 1) of total time; increasing M shrinks this fraction, at the cost of holding activations for more in-flight microbatches (or paying recomputation).
Pipeline parallelism reduces the wall-clock time of a single microbatch's forward+backward pass by a factor of P relative to single-GPU execution, so the bubble is a negligible overhead in practice.
The bubble is a compiler artifact; an optimizing compiler can eliminate it completely for any P and M by fusing stages into a single kernel.

explanation: In GPipe, the pipeline needs P-1 steps to fill and P-1 to drain, giving a total time of (P-1) + M + (P-1) = P + M - 1 stage-times for M microbatches, of which (P-1) is spent doing useful work per stage and (P-1) is fill/drain — hence bubble fraction (P-1)/(P + M - 1). Larger M dilutes the bubble but keeps more activations alive (memory cost). Pipelining does not shorten a single microbatch's latency — it raises throughput.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: bubble fraction depends on M, not just P.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: canonical GPipe bubble fraction, plus the memory trade-off.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: pipeline parallelism raises throughput, not single-microbatch latency.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: bubble is intrinsic to fill/drain, not a compiler artifact.

assumptions: Communication is overlapped or negligible relative to stage compute.
nonImplications: Does not imply that 1F1B or interleaved pipelines have the same bubble; they change the constant but not the fundamental fill/drain requirement.
Does not imply larger M is always better; memory pressure eventually forces recomputation or activation offloading.
